source_text: Contra haec nos quotidie disputamus et ideo nolumus praevaricatoribus adhibere consensum, quia dicimus liberum arbitrium in omnibus esse naturaliter nec Adae peccato perire potuisse, quod omnium Scripturarum auctoritate firmatur.
pass_a_gloss: Against these things we dispute daily and therefore we are unwilling to apply consent to prevaricators, because we say that free decision is in all by nature and could not perish by Adam's sin, which is confirmed by the authority of all the Scriptures.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium

pass_b_english: We argue against these things every day. We refuse to agree with those who do wrong, because we say that free will belongs to everyone by nature and could not have been destroyed by Adam's sin. The authority of all the Scriptures confirms this.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (Letter to Rome, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 1); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
